description: Factors, multiples, divisibility rules and primes

lessons.title: What is a Factor?
lessons.intro: A factor is a number that divides another number exactly, leaving no remainder.
explanation: The factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4 and 8.
Every number has at least two factors: 1 and itself.
Factors always come in pairs that multiply to the number.
lessons.rule: A factor divides a number with no remainder.
lessons.tip: 1 is a factor of every number.

steps.text: Test if a number divides exactly.

lessons.title: Factor Pairs
lessons.intro: Finding factor pairs is a neat way to list every factor without missing any.
explanation: When a pair repeats (4x4), that factor is counted once.
Pairs guarantee you catch them all.
lessons.rule: List factor pairs from 1 upward.
lessons.tip: Stop when the pair values meet.

lessons.title: Counting Factors
lessons.intro: Some numbers have many factors, others very few.
explanation: 24 has factors 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 — eight of them.
A prime number has exactly two factors.
More factors usually means a 'friendlier' number for sharing.
lessons.rule: Count factors by listing every pair.
lessons.tip: Perfect squares have an odd number of factors.

lessons.title: The Smallest and Largest Factor
lessons.intro: Every number's smallest factor is 1 and its largest factor is itself.
explanation: Smallest factor of any number is 1.
Largest factor of 45 (other than 45) is 15.
The second-largest factor pairs with the second-smallest.
lessons.rule: Smallest factor is 1; largest is the number itself.
lessons.tip: The biggest 'other' factor = number / smallest prime factor.

lessons.title: Special Factor Facts
lessons.intro: Factors hide some lovely patterns worth knowing.
explanation: The factors of 36 are 1,2,3,4,6,9,12,18,36 — nine factors.
6 is a 'perfect number': its factors 1,2,3 add up to 6.
Exploring factors reveals maths magic.
lessons.rule: A perfect number equals the sum of its smaller factors.

lessons.title: What is a Multiple?
lessons.intro: A multiple of a number is what you get when you multiply it by a whole number.
explanation: The 5th multiple of 4 is 20.
Multiples are just the times-table of a number.
lessons.rule: A multiple = number x a whole number.
lessons.tip: The multiples of n are its times-table.

steps.text: The nth multiple is n times the number.

lessons.title: Multiples Never End
lessons.intro: Unlike factors, multiples go on forever — you can always find a bigger one.
explanation: Multiples of 3: 3,6,9,12,... endless.
The 7th multiple of 3 is 21.
The smallest multiple of any number is the number itself.
lessons.rule: Multiples are infinite; the smallest is the number itself.

lessons.title: Recognising Multiples
lessons.intro: You can check if a number is a multiple of another by dividing.
explanation: Is 24 a multiple of 6? 24 / 6 = 4, yes.
If the division is exact, it is a multiple.
Being a multiple of n means n is a factor of it.
lessons.rule: If it divides exactly, it is a multiple.
lessons.tip: Multiples and factors are opposites of each other.

lessons.title: Multiples in Groups
lessons.intro: Multiples help when counting equal groups.
explanation: 7 chairs per row, 6 rows: 7 x 6 = 42 chairs.
The total is a multiple of the group size.
Repeated addition and multiples go together.
lessons.rule: Equal groups give multiples of the group size.
lessons.tip: Total = group size x number of groups.

lessons.title: Counting Multiples
lessons.intro: We can count how many multiples of a number fall in a range.
explanation: Multiples of 5 from 1 to 50: 5,10,...,50 — that is 10 of them.
Divide the top of the range by the number.
The first multiple over 50 for 8 is 56.
lessons.rule: Count multiples by dividing the range end.

lessons.title: Divisibility by 2, 5, 10
lessons.intro: Some numbers can be tested for division just by looking at their last digit.
explanation: A number is divisible by 2 if it ends in 0,2,4,6,8 (even).
Divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.
Divisible by 10 if it ends in 0.
lessons.rule: Last digit tells divisibility by 2, 5 and 10.

steps.text: 6 is even, so 126 is divisible by 2.

lessons.title: Divisibility by 3 and 9
lessons.intro: For 3 and 9 we add the digits — a neat trick!
explanation: Divisible by 3 if the digit sum is divisible by 3.
123: 1+2+3=6, divisible by 3.
Divisible by 9 if the digit sum is divisible by 9.
lessons.rule: Add the digits to test 3 and 9.
lessons.tip: If the digit sum works, the number does too.

lessons.title: Divisibility by 4
lessons.intro: A number is divisible by 4 if its last TWO digits form a number divisible by 4.
explanation: 128: last two digits 28, and 28 / 4 = 7, so yes.
You can ignore all the earlier digits.
This works because 100 is divisible by 4.
lessons.rule: Check the last two digits for divisibility by 4.

lessons.title: Divisibility by 8
lessons.intro: For 8, check the last THREE digits.
explanation: 1000 is divisible by 8 (1000 / 8 = 125).
Only the last three digits matter.
This works because 1000 is divisible by 8.
lessons.rule: Check the last three digits for divisibility by 8.

lessons.title: Using the Rules Together
lessons.intro: Combine the rules to test bigger numbers quickly without long division.
explanation: 234: ends in 4 (div by 2) and digit sum 9 (div by 9).
So 234 is divisible by 2, 3, 6 and 9.
The rules save a lot of time.
lessons.rule: Combine rules to test many divisors fast.
lessons.tip: Divisible by 2 and 3 means divisible by 6.

lessons.title: Prime Numbers
lessons.intro: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Primes are the atoms of maths!
explanation: 7 is prime: only 1 and 7 divide it.
The first primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ...
2 is the only even prime number.
lessons.rule: A prime has exactly two factors.

steps.text: Check for factors other than 1 and itself.

lessons.title: Composite Numbers
lessons.intro: A composite number has more than two factors.
explanation: 9 is composite: 1, 3, 9.
Every whole number above 1 is prime or composite.
1 is neither prime nor composite.
lessons.rule: Composite numbers have more than two factors.
lessons.tip: 1 is special: not prime, not composite.

lessons.title: Is It Prime?
lessons.intro: To test if a number is prime, try dividing by small primes.
explanation: Test 29: not divisible by 2,3,5 — so it is prime.
If no small prime divides it, it is prime.
You only need to test primes up to its square root.
lessons.rule: If no prime up to the square root divides it, it is prime.

lessons.title: The Number 1 and 2
lessons.intro: Two special cases trip people up: 1 and 2.
explanation: 1 has only one factor, so it is NOT prime.
2 is prime and is the only even prime.
Knowing these avoids common mistakes.
lessons.rule: 1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime.

lessons.title: Counting Primes
lessons.intro: Primes become rarer as numbers get bigger, but they never stop.
explanation: Primes under 10: 2,3,5,7 — four of them.
Primes under 20: add 11,13,17,19 — eight in all.
The largest prime under 30 is 29.
lessons.rule: Primes thin out but continue forever.
lessons.tip: List them carefully; do not skip 2.

lessons.title: Prime Factorisation
lessons.intro: Breaking a number into primes gives its unique prime factorisation.
explanation: Divide by the smallest prime over and over.
Every number has exactly one prime factorisation.
lessons.rule: Prime factorisation = a number written as primes multiplied.

steps.text: Divide repeatedly by the smallest prime.

lessons.title: Factor Trees
lessons.intro: A factor tree is a picture that helps break a number into primes.
explanation: 8 splits into 2 and 4, then 4 into 2 and 2.
So 8 = 2 x 2 x 2.
Keep branching until every leaf is prime.
lessons.rule: A factor tree ends when all leaves are prime.

lessons.title: Largest and Smallest Prime Factor
lessons.intro: Among a number's prime factors, we can pick the biggest or smallest.
explanation: 30 = 2x3x5: smallest prime factor 2, largest 5.
35 = 5x7: smallest 5, largest 7.
The smallest prime factor divides the number first.
lessons.rule: Identify the smallest and largest prime factors.

lessons.title: Counting Prime Factors
lessons.intro: We can count prime factors, with or without repeats.
explanation: 24 = 2x2x2x3 — four prime factors with repetition.
16 = 2x2x2x2 — four twos.
Repetition counts each copy.
lessons.rule: Count every prime, including repeats.

lessons.title: Prime Power Master
lessons.intro: Combine factor trees and products to solve any prime puzzle.
explanation: Multiply chosen primes to build new numbers.
Prime factors unlock HCF and LCM too.
lessons.rule: Master prime factors to tackle HCF, LCM and more.
